transcript.answer: Only partly. Sending the token as the WebSocket subprotocol keeps it out of the URL and request line, so a URL-based access log won't capture it. It is not fully safe from logging, though. The token still travels in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` request header. An ingress log with header capture, a proxy trace, or a debug dump of the request can record it there. The original claim that this avoids log exposure was only half true. Issue #150 found that the server echoed the token back in the 101 response headers and kept it on the socket object. It was fixed so the server answers only the reserved marker `hal.v1`. The client offers `hal.v1, <token>`, and the token appears in no response header and is not held on the socket's `protocol` property. The request-header exposure remains. The docs are meant to say so, and to list every place a credential exists so operators can configure log redaction. The requirement is that no value offered in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is written to any log.
